abstract: "Mental rotation — the ability to mentally transform an object's orientation in space — is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive and developmental psychology, yet the cross-cultural generalizability of mental rotation tasks in children remains largely untested. The present study examines data from 568 children aged 5–12 across three culturally diverse sites (Canada, Germany, and Colombia) participating in the Learning Variability Network Exchange (LEVANTE), addressing three research questions that build a layered case for the task's cross-cultural validity. First, multi-group item response theory supported scalar measurement invariance across sites, indicating that the same item features drive difficulty regardless of cultural context. Second, the canonical angular disparity effect first reported by Shepard and Metzler (1971) replicated across all three sites for 3D stimuli, with a significant but attenuated effect for 2D stimuli. Third, an exploratory clustering analysis identified three profiles of task engagement ranging from disengagement to effective feature-matching and analog rotation, though the boundary between the latter two profiles was not robustly recoverable within sites. Taken together, these findings establish that the LEVANTE mental rotation task captures a consistent and spatially-driven construct across culturally diverse samples of children — a necessary precondition for using cross-cultural data to understand why children vary in spatial reasoning."

# Introduction

From fitting puzzle pieces together at age threee to navigating complex diagrams in school, spatial reasoning underpins a broad array of cognitive achievements — and children differ substantially in how these skills develop. Such variability is detectable early, across a wide range of spatial tasks in primary school-aged children [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and its consequences are far-reaching: spatial ability predicts outcomes spanning creative domains such as music [@padulo2020effects; @hetland2000learning] and the visual arts [@kell2013creativity; @winner2013relationship], mathematical achievement [@gunderson2012relation], science learning [@gilligan2020first], and long-term educational and occupational outcomes in STEM fields [@wai2009spatial]. Understanding what drives this variability is therefore a question of both theoretical and practical importance. The present study takes a step toward that goal by examining children's performance on a mental rotation task across three culturally diverse countries, asking both what is consistent across children and what varies.

Spatial reasoning encompasses abilities for representing, transforming, and reasoning about visuospatial information [@lohman1996spatial]. Rather than a single unified capacity, it is better understood as a family of related but distinguishable skills, including mental rotation, spatial visualization, perspective-taking, and navigation, that differ in the type of spatial information involved and the cognitive operations required [@uttal2013malleability; @newcombe2018three]. Skills are organized along two dimensions: whether the spatial relations are intrinsic to an object or extrinsic between objects, and whether the task requires dynamic mental transformation or only static representation [@uttal2013malleability]. Mental rotation — the focus of the present study — falls in the intrinsic-dynamic quadrant of this framework, involving the mental transformation of an object's orientation in space.

Mental rotation is the ability to mentally transform an object by rotating it in space to predict how it would appear from a different orientation or viewpoint [@shepard1971mental]. It is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive and developmental psychology, in part because it yields one of the most robust and replicable findings in the field: response times increase approximately linearly with the angular disparity between two 3D objects, suggesting that mental rotation operates as a spatially continuous process rather than a discrete rule-based one [@shepard1971mental; @cooper1973chronometric]. We return to this finding in detail below.

Mental rotation ability develops across a protracted period beginning in infancy. Precursors of successful rotation are detectable in the first year of life [@frick2014development; @moore2008mental], and performance on explicit rotation tasks improves substantially between ages 3-12  [@frick2013development; @marmor1975development], with continued refinement into adolescence. This extended developmental trajectory makes the primary school years, ages 5-12, a particularly informative window for studying how mental rotation skills are acquired and how they vary across children.

The standard mental rotation task, as developed by @shepard1971mental, presents participants with pairs of objects at varying angular disparities and asks them to judge whether the objects are identical or mirror-reversed. Response time and accuracy are the key dependent variables. While this paradigm has generated decades of consistent findings, performance on the task does not necessarily reflect mental rotation per se — participants may instead rely on alternative spatial strategies that produce similar accuracy and response time patterns. Research with adults suggests that solvers draw on a range of strategies, spanning a holistic-analytic continuum [@gluck2003spatial]. At the holistic end, the stimulus is transformed as an integrated mental representation — the so-called "pure rotation" or "analog rotation" approach. At the analytic end, solvers decompose the object into sub-components and verify features sequentially, a more piecemeal strategy that places greater demands on working memory [@just1985cognitive; @khooshabeh2013individual]. Strategy selection is not fixed: individuals differ in their preferred approach, and the same individual may shift strategies depending on task demands such as the complexity of the stimulus or the degree of angular disparity [@nazareth2019strategy]. Importantly, far less is known about which strategies children employ when solving mental rotation problems, and whether strategy use varies with age, ability, or cultural context. This question motivates the exploratory component of the present study, which we describe below.

The vast majority of developmental research on mental rotation has been conducted with children from Western, educated populations [@davis2019spatial; @peters2006mental], raising questions about whether findings about its developmental trajectory, psychometric properties, and underlying cognitive processes generalize beyond the populations in which they were established.

The limited cross-cultural evidence that does exist offers a mixed picture. A large-scale study of 3,367 students across Canada, Germany, and Japan found that a male performance advantage on mental rotation was consistent across all three nations, suggesting some cross-cultural robustness in group-level patterns [@peters2006mental]. However, cross-cultural comparisons of children specifically are rare. One notable exception compared children in the Ivory Coast and Switzerland and found that while both groups showed evidence of mental rotation, Swiss children demonstrated substantially higher speed and accuracy. Critically, age predicted performance in the Swiss group but not in the Ivorean group, suggesting that the developmental trajectory of mental rotation, not just its overall level, may differ across cultural contexts [@nunez1998mental]. More recent work in non-WEIRD (i.e., Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations has shown that environmental and cultural factors — including access to formal schooling, freedom to explore the physical environment, and culturally-specific spatial practices — can substantially shape both the level and the pattern of spatial performance in children [@davis2019spatial; @davis2021cultural].

Taken together, this evidence highlights two distinct but related gaps. First, we have limited data on whether mental rotation tasks developed and validated in Western samples are measuring the same underlying construct when administered to children in different cultural contexts. Second, even where cross-cultural comparisons have been made, they have rarely examined whether the core cognitive signatures of mental rotation replicate across diverse populations of children. The linear relationship between reaction time and angular disparity — one of the most robust findings in cognitive psychology — has been demonstrated repeatedly in Western adult samples, but its replication in children across culturally diverse sites remains largely untested. Beyond these two gaps, relatively little is known about the cognitive strategies children employ when solving mental rotation problems, and whether these vary across cultural contexts — a question we explore tentatively here. Addressing these gaps is not an end in itself — it is a necessary precondition for using cross-cultural data to understand why children vary in spatial reasoning.

Our first research question asks whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task achieves measurement invariance across culturally diverse sites — that is, whether it captures the same underlying construct regardless of where it is administered. Our second asks whether performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli in the way theory predicts, using the angular disparity effect as the key benchmark: as the angular difference between two objects increases, so too should the time required to judge whether they match. If children across three culturally diverse sites show this same systematic pattern, this constitutes good evidence that the task is engaging the spatial demands it was designed to capture. Alongside these two primary research questions, we tentatively explore a third: whether children draw on different cognitive strategies when solving mental rotation problems, and whether this varies across contexts. We treat this component with appropriate caution, given the limitations of the data for addressing it directly.

## The Present Study

The present study uses data from the Learning Variability Network Exchange (LEVANTE), an international research collaboration designed to capture how children's learning and development vary across ages and cultural contexts. LEVANTE's central aim is to build a large, openly shared dataset of children's cognitive development across diverse settings, with a particular focus on individual variability — what differs across children, and why. Data were collected from three geographically and culturally diverse pilot sites: uniandes-co, mpieva-de, and western-ca.Here we use data from a single task in the LEVANTE battery: a mental rotation task developed using item response theory, which allows directly comparable ability estimates to be derived across children who completed different subsets of items [@Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks].

We address our three research questions in turn. First, we examine measurement invariance across the three pilot sites. Second, we test whether the canonical Shepard-Metzler angular disparity effect replicates across all three sites in children aged 5 to 12. Third, in an exploratory analysis, we ask whether meaningful variation in cognitive strategy can be identified from trial-level behavioral signatures — approaching this not as a search for discrete strategy types, but as an attempt to characterize the continuum of engagement with the spatial demands of the task. Taken together, these three questions move from psychometric structure (measurement invariance), to process-level validity (angular disparity effect), to profiles of engagement (cognitive strategies) — building a layered case for the task's cross-cultural validity.

# Methods

## Participants

Data for the present study were drawn from three pilot sites participating in LEVANTE: uniandes-co, mpieva-de, and western-ca. Collectively, these sites supported task localization and technical implementation, iterative piloting, and deployment in varied testing contexts. The resulting pilot datasets enabled preliminary evaluation of construct validity, measurement invariance, test–retest reliability, and calibration for computer-adaptive administration, as well as descriptive assessment of age-related differences across the targeted constructs (refer to @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks for a full description).

### uniandes-co

The Universidad de Los Andes team carried out school-based data collection in Colombia, working with four schools in Bogotá and two public schools in the rural departments of Caquetá and Boyacá. Schools were selected pragmatically from institutions that had previously collaborated with the university. In Bogotá, three schools were affiliated with two family compensation funds and one was operated by a charter-school organisation. Across locations, participating schools largely served children from low-income and lower-middle-income backgrounds. Testing was conducted on tablets provided by the research team using a group-administration format, with group sizes adjusted by age (larger groups for older children; smaller groups for younger children).

### mpieva-de

At the mpieva-de site, the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology implemented a remote, family-based assessment protocol. Families were recruited via an existing registry of Leipzig residents and were contacted by telephone to invite participation. Families who enrolled were given login details and completed the assigned LEVANTE tasks at home using their own computer or tablet.

### western-ca

The Western University (Ontario) team recruited children from the surrounding community, primarily via online outreach (e.g., Facebook advertisements and posts in community groups), complemented by physical flyers and announcements distributed through local school newsletters. Families self-enrolled by registering their interest in a participant database. Children were assessed individually by a researcher in a dedicated on-campus testing space.

## Measure

The LEVANTE mental rotation task is adapted from @frick2013development. On each trial, children view a target image (e.g., a rabbit) and then choose between two alternatives (e.g., two rabbit silhouettes): one alternative is the same object shown at a different orientation, whereas the other is a non-matching foil (see @fig-mrot-example-items). Children indicate which option corresponds to the target, and their accuracy (correct/incorrect) and response time are recorded. Angular disparity is manipulated across trials (e.g., 40°, 80°, 120°, 160°), producing systematic effects on performance. Stimuli include 2D animal figures (ducks and rabbits) and more challenging 3D geometric shapes drawn from the classic Shepard and Metzler (1971) set. The task has recently been revised to include polygons as stimuli of intermediate difficulty between the 2D figures and 3D shapes; however, these are not included in the current analyses due to insufficient data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mrot-example-items
#| fig-cap: "Example items for 2D and 3D rotation"
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: "center"

knitr::include_graphics("mrot_item_examples.pdf")
```
\clearpage
The nine core tasks in LEVANTE, including mental rotation, were initially designed in English and then subsequently adapted for Spanish and German following a set of internationalization procedures in collaboration with researchers at the uniandes-co and mpieva-de sites, respectively. We began with AI-generated translations of all verbal materials, including task instructions, items, and other key terminology such as encouragement phrases that appear throughout the core tasks; we used both DeepL and Google Translate for these initial translations. Translations were managed using Crowdin, a platform that allows translators to view task stimuli and text simultaneously, ensuring translations are appropriate in context. A professional translator then reviewed and edited the AI translations for general grammatical correctness and appropriateness. Materials were next reviewed by a researcher who was a native speaker of the relevant language and dialect, confirming that the materials were clear and appropriate for the specific task. We then conducted back translation using AI translation tools to verify semantic and conceptual equivalence and to flag items needing further review by native speakers.

The mental rotation task has already been implemented in a computer-adaptive task (CAT) format. In the adaptive version, participant ability is summarized by a latent proficiency estimate (theta) that is re-estimated after each response. The updated theta then guides selection of the next item so that it is appropriately challenging for each individual child. This trial-by-trial targeting typically makes the task more engaging and increases measurement efficiency, enabling reliable ability estimation with fewer administered items. Refer to @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks for more information on the CAT versions of all LEVANTE tasks.

Site-level sampling characteristics are described in @tbl-participants. Due to de-identification protocols, individual-level demographic data including gender and socioeconomic indicators are not currently available. Three participants with ages above 12 years were excluded as they were outside the target age range (5-12 years), leaving a final sample of n = 568.

Although we use psychometric modelling to place children's performance on a common scale, LEVANTE is not designed to support site-level performance comparisons — sites vary substantially in sampling, recruitment, and test administration in ways that heavily confound absolute comparisons. Descriptive patterns that appear to reflect cross-site differences in performance should not be interpreted as such.

# Results

## Cross-Cultural Measurement Invariance of the Mental Rotation Task

Our first research question asked whether the mental rotation task measures the same underlying construct across all three sites — that is, whether it achieves measurement invariance. To  evaluate measurement invariance, we used multi-group IRT [@putnick2016measurement]. Multi-group models supported scalar invariance under a 2PL model, indicating that item difficulty is aligned across sites and that children in each country are being placed on a comparable latent scale. Practically, this means the groups share the same relative ordering of item difficulty — items with larger rotation angles and 3D items are consistently more difficult across all three countries (see @tbl-mrot-2pl-scalar). 

```{r}
#| label: irt-anova
#| include: false

# IRT model output - import object
github_dir <- file.path(path.expand("~"), "Documents", "GitHub")
task_anova_path <- file.path(github_dir, "levante-pilots", "02_scoring_outputs", "task_anova.rds")

stopifnot(file.exists(task_anova_path))
task_anova <- readRDS(task_anova_path)
#colnames(task_anova)
#table(task_anova$itemtype)

# extract
mrot_2pl_scalar <- task_anova %>%
  filter(task == "mrot", itemtype == "2pl", invariance == "scalar")
mrot_2pl_scalar
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mrot-2pl-scalar
#| tbl-cap: "**Model fit indices for 2PL scalar invariance models.** Note: 2PL = 2-parameter logistic model; scalar invariance indicates that item intercepts and loadings are constrained across groups."
#| echo: false

mrot_2pl_scalar %>%
  transmute(
    Task       = task,
    Factors    = nfact,
    Model      = itemtype,
    Invariance = invariance,
    logLik     = logLik,
    AIC        = AIC,
    BIC        = BIC,
    `# params` = df
  ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  # Ensures the gt title area is clear and doesn't overlap the Quarto caption
  tab_header(title = md("")) %>% 
  fmt_number(columns = c(logLik, AIC, BIC), decimals = 2) %>%
  fmt_number(columns = `# params`, decimals = 0, use_seps = FALSE) %>%
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(Task, Factors, Model, Invariance, `# params`)) %>%
  cols_align(align = "right",  columns = c(logLik, AIC, BIC)) %>%
  tab_options(
    #table.font.size = px(12), # Increased slightly for better legibility
    table.width = pct(100),   # Ensures it fills the page width nicely
    data_row.padding = px(3)   # Tighter row spacing often looks better for stats
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-item-diff

# Load configural parameters
mrot_configural <- all_coefs |>

# pivot wide
mrot_wide_d <- mrot_configural |>
  dplyr::select(item, group, d) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = d) |>
  dplyr::mutate(item_label = item |>
                  stringr::str_remove("mrot_2d_") |>
                  stringr::str_remove("mrot_3d_") |>
                  stringr::str_replace("_", " ") |>
                  stringr::str_replace("(\\d+)$", "\\1°"))

plot_scatter <- function(data, x_var, y_var, x_lab, y_lab) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = .data[[x_var]], y = .data[[y_var]],
                   label = item_label)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1,
                linetype = "dashed", colour = pal$grey) +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(size = 2.8,
                    max.overlaps = Inf,
                    box.padding = 0.5,
                    point.padding = 0.3,
                    na.rm = TRUE) +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-2.5, 4), ylim = c(-2.5, 4)) +
    labs(x = x_lab, y = y_lab)
}

p1 <- plot_scatter(mrot_wide_d, "Canada", "Germany",   "Canada", "Germany")
p2 <- plot_scatter(mrot_wide_d, "Canada", "Colombia",  "Canada", "Colombia")
p3 <- plot_scatter(mrot_wide_d, "Germany", "Colombia", "Germany", "Colombia")

(p1 | p2 | p3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Item Difficulty Parameters Across Sites (Configural Model)",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 12))
  )

# checks
all_coefs |>
  dplyr::filter(task == "mrot", itemtype == "2pl", invariance == "configural") |>
  dplyr::count(subset, group)
```

@fig-dev-trends plots participants' mental rotation ability estimates (IRT theta) against age, with curves by site modeled using generalized additive models (GAMs). GAMs allow the developmental association with age to be non-linear, capturing periods of more rapid change and relative flattening without imposing a fixed form. Across all three sites, theta increases with age, indicating that the task captures developmental change consistently across cultural contexts. The dispersion of points within age bands underscores substantial individual variability in ability among same-aged children. We next turn to our second research question: whether performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli in the way theory predicts. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-dev-trends
#| fig-cap: "**Developmental trajectories of mental rotation ability across sites.** Points represent individual children's IRT-estimated ability (θ); curves are GAM-smoothed age trends with 95% confidence intervals. Vertical offsets between sites should not be interpreted as performance differences; LEVANTE sites differ in sampling and recruitment in ways that heavily confound absolute comparisons."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot(mrot_df, aes(x = age, y = metric_value, colour = site_label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x, k = 5), se = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  labs(
    x      = "Age (years)",
    y      = "Ability (theta)",
    colour = "Site"
  )
```

```{r}
#| include: false

mrot_rt_trial <- all_sum_scores %>%
  dplyr::filter(item_task == "mrot") %>%
  dplyr::select(site, data) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(data) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    correct = dplyr::case_when(
      is.logical(correct) ~ as.integer(correct),
      TRUE ~ as.integer(as.numeric(correct))
    ),
    rt_s   = as.numeric(rt_numeric) / 1000,
    log_rt = log(rt_s)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(rt_s), rt_s > 0)

# age per run 
run_ages <- run_data %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    user_id,
    run_id,
    age = as.numeric(age)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(is.finite(age))
```

```{r}
  left_join(run_ages, by = c("user_id", "run_id")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(age), age < 13) %>%
  mutate(
    age_group  = cut(age, breaks = c(5, 7, 9, 12),
                     include.lowest = TRUE, right = TRUE),
    item_group = factor(item_group),   # 2D vs 3D
    site       = factor(site),
    angle_sc   = as.numeric(scale(angle)),  # scale for model stability
    log_rt     = log(rt_s)
  ) %>%
  filter(is.finite(log_rt), correct == 1)  # correct trials only, finite RTs
```

```{r}
# --- 3D stimuli: main test of angular disparity effect ---

mrot_3d <- mrot_lme_data %>%
  filter(item_group == "3d") %>%

# check size
nrow(mrot_3d)

# now fit all models on the same object
m_3d_main <- lmer(

)

  log_rt ~ angle_sc * age_group + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
  data = mrot_3d, REML = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

m_3d_full <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_sc * site * age_group + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
  data = mrot_3d, REML = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

anova_3d <- anova(m_3d_main, m_3d_site, m_3d_age, m_3d_full)

mrot_2d <- mrot_lme_data %>%
  filter(item_group == "2d") %>%
  filter(!is.na(site), !is.na(age_group), !is.na(angle_sc), !is.na(log_rt)) %>%
  droplevels()

nrow(mrot_2d)

m_2d_main <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_sc + (1 + angle_sc | user_id),
  data = mrot_2d, REML = FALSE,

)
```

## Angular disparity and the RT–angle relationship

Our second research question asked whether performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli in the way theory predicts — specifically, whether the canonical angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental replicates across all three sites. To test this formally, we fitted linear mixed-effects models predicting log RT from rotation angle, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for angle (Satterthwaite's method for degrees of freedom). We standardized rotation angle to have a mean of zero and standard deviation (SD) of 1 prior to analysis, such that coefficients reflect change in log RT per SD increase in angle rather than per degree. We excluded CAT trials from all models as adaptive item selection introduces a systematic confound between ability and angle exposure.

For 3D stimuli, there was a strong positive effect of rotation angle (β = `r round(beta_3d_main, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_3d_main, 2)`, t(`r round(df_3d_main, 1)`) = `r round(t_3d_main, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_3d_main)`), confirming that response times increased systematically with angular disparity across the full sample. Adding site as a moderator significantly improved model fit (χ²(`r anova_site_df`) = `r round(anova_site_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_site_p)`), indicating that the magnitude of the angle slope differed across sites. The angle slope did not differ significantly between Germany and Colombia (β = `r round(beta_site_co, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_site_co, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_site_co)`), but was significantly shallower in Canada than Germany (β = `r round(beta_site_ca, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_site_ca, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_site_ca)`). Age group did not independently moderate the angle slope (χ²(`r anova_age_df`) = `r round(anova_age_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_age_p)`). The shallower angle slope in Canada likely reflects some combination of sampling and procedural factors: a smaller sample yields less precise estimates, and the distinctive testing format — individual on-campus assessment by a researcher — may have introduced procedural differences that compressed RT variability.

For 2D stimuli, we observed a significant but smaller positive angle effect (β = `r round(beta_2d_main, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_main, 2)`, t(`r round(df_2d_main, 1)`) = `r round(t_2d_main, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_main)`). A combined model confirmed that the angle slope was significantly steeper for 3D than 2D stimuli (β difference = `r round(beta_diff, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_diff, 2)`, χ²(`r anova_combined_df`) = `r round(anova_combined_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_combined_p)`), with the 3D slope (β = `r round(beta_3d_comb, 2)`) approximately `r round(beta_3d_comb / beta_2d_comb, 1)` times larger than the 2D slope (β = `r round(beta_2d_comb, 2)`).

@fig-rt-angle-per-run-no-cat plots mean reaction times (±95% confidence intervals) as a function of rotation angle, stratified by age group (5–7, 7–9, and 9–12 years) and site, with separate series by stimulus and item type (2D vs 3D). See @apx-irt-ability-age for the raw per-run data underlying these trends.

\clearpage

## Within-Person Dynamics

Having established that 3D stimuli elicit a clear angular disparity effect while 2D stimuli do to a lesser extent, we next asked a complementary question: whether children show sensitivity to task demands as they unfold in real time — specifically, whether reaction times shift systematically at the transition from 2D to 3D stimuli, and whether practice effects are detectable within blocks. To isolate time-on-task effects from item-driven RT changes, we residualized log-RTs on angle, stimulus, and item type prior to analysis.

```{r}
#| label: fig-within-person-trials
#| fig-cap: "**Trial-level Reaction Time Dynamics (angle-residualised).** Mean residual log-RT across trials for each non-adaptive site ±SE. The dashed line marks the 2D→3D transition. Re-test and CAT data removed."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

# prep: remove CAT data
trial_resid_data <- mrot_rt_trial_no_retest %>%
  left_join(cat_data, by = c("user_id", "run_id")) %>%
  filter(adaptive == FALSE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(log_rt), correct == 1) %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = stringr::str_extract(item, "^[a-z]+"),
    angle    = as.integer(stringr::str_extract(item, "(?<=_)\\d+"))
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(angle), !is.na(stimulus), !is.na(item_group))

# residualise log_rt on angle + stimulus + item_group
resid_model <- lm(log_rt ~ angle + stimulus + item_group, 
                  data = trial_resid_data)

trial_resid_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(log_rt_resid = residuals(resid_model))

# add block variable
transition_trial <- 48 

trial_resid_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  mutate(
site_label = dplyr::recode(site, !!!setNames(names(site_labels), unname(site_labels))),    
block = if_else(trial_number < transition_trial, "2D", "3D")
  )

# plot
ggplot(trial_resid_data, 
       aes(x = trial_number, y = log_rt_resid, 
           color = site_label, fill = site_label)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 1.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = interaction(site_label, block)),
              method = "loess", span = 0.75, se = TRUE, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = transition_trial, linetype = "dashed",
             color = pal$grey, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = transition_trial + 1, y = Inf,
           label = "Start of 3D block", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = site_pal_labelled) +
  labs(
    x     = "Trial Number",
    y     = "Residual reaction time",
    color = "Site",
    fill  = "Site"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: within-person-models
#| include: false

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

# centre trial number within each block so the intercept at transition is interpretable
within_person_data <- trial_resid_data %>%
  left_join(run_ages, by = c("user_id", "run_id")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(age), age < 13) %>%
  mutate(
    block         = factor(block, levels = c("2D", "3D")),
    # trial number centred within block
    trial_c       = trial_number - transition_trial,
    site          = factor(site)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(trial_number), !is.na(log_rt_resid))

# Model 1: continuous trial slope only — no special status for transition
m_wp_continuous <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + (1 + trial_c | user_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 2: add block as main effect — tests for discontinuous jump at transition
m_wp_jump <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c + block + (1 + trial_c | user_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Model 3: add trial × block interaction — tests whether slope changes after transition
m_wp_slope <- lmer(
  log_rt_resid ~ trial_c * block + (1 + trial_c | user_id),
  data    = within_person_data,
  REML    = FALSE,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# model comparisons
anova_wp_jump  <- anova(m_wp_continuous, m_wp_jump)   # is there a jump?
anova_wp_slope <- anova(m_wp_jump, m_wp_slope)         # does slope also change?

# extract key numbers
wp_coefs       <- coef(summary(m_wp_slope))

# block jump (intercept shift at transition)
beta_wp_block  <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_block    <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_block     <- wp_coefs["block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# within-block trial slope (2D block)
beta_wp_trial  <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Estimate"]
se_wp_trial    <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_trial     <- wp_coefs["trial_c", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# interaction: does slope differ in 3D block?
beta_wp_int    <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Estimate"]
se_wp_int      <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Std. Error"]
p_wp_int       <- wp_coefs["trial_c:block3D", "Pr(>|t|)"]

# anova numbers for inline reporting
wp_jump_chisq  <- anova_wp_jump$Chisq[2]
wp_jump_df     <- anova_wp_jump$Df[2]
wp_jump_p      <- anova_wp_jump[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]

wp_slope_chisq <- anova_wp_slope$Chisq[2]
wp_slope_df    <- anova_wp_slope$Df[2]
wp_slope_p     <- anova_wp_slope[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2]

```
\clearpage

@fig-within-person-trials plots mean residual log-RT across trials for each site. To test for a discontinuous shift in RT at the 2D→3D block transition and for within-block practice effects, we fitted a series of mixed-effects models predicting residual log-RT from trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes.

First, a model including a block indicator (2D vs 3D) significantly improved fit over a continuous trial-slope model (χ²(`r wp_jump_df`) = `r round(wp_jump_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_jump_p)`), confirming that the increase in RT at the 2D→3D transition is discontinuous rather than a continuation of a gradual trend. The block coefficient indicates a sudden upward shift in residual RT at trial 48 (β = `r round(beta_wp_block, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_block, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_block)`), consistent with children recalibrating their processing demands at the block boundary rather than adapting incrementally.

Second, within each block, RTs decreased across trials, indicating a practice effect operating independently of angular disparity (β = `r round(beta_wp_trial, 4)`, SE = `r round(se_wp_trial, 4)`, p `r fmt_p(p_wp_trial)`). Adding a trial × block interaction `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, "significantly improved model fit", "did not significantly improve model fit")` 
(χ²(`r wp_slope_df`) = `r round(wp_slope_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(wp_slope_p)`) `r ifelse(wp_slope_p < .05, paste0(", with the within-block acceleration differing between the 2D and 3D blocks (β = ", round(beta_wp_int, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_wp_int, 3), ", p ", fmt_p(p_wp_int), ")"), "")`. Both patterns — the discontinuous block transition and the within-block acceleration — were qualitatively consistent across all three sites, further extending the cross-cultural consistency observed in the angular disparity analysis.

```{r}
#| label: strategy-analysis-prep
#| results: "hide"

# ability
ability_user <- all_scores %>% 
  filter(item_task == "mrot", metric_type == "ability") %>% 
  mutate(
    metric_value = as.numeric(metric_value),
    age = as.numeric(age)
  ) %>%
  group_by(site, user_id) %>%
  summarise(
    ability = mean(metric_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    age     = first(age),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Prepare trial-level data for the rich model
mrot_rich_data <- mrot_rt_trial_no_retest %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus = str_extract(item, "^[a-z]+"),
    angle    = as.integer(str_extract(item, "\\d+")),
    stimulus = as.factor(stimulus),
    angle_s  = as.numeric(scale(angle)),
    trial_s  = as.numeric(scale(trial_number))
  )

# set sum-to-zero contrasts - by default, R uses treatment contrasts (Duck = reference). 
# This makes the "Angle" slope represent only Ducks (which is flat for everyone).
# Setting sum contrasts ensures the "Angle" slope represents the grand mean slope across all stimuli.
contrasts(mrot_rich_data$stimulus) <- contr.sum(levels(mrot_rich_data$stimulus))
m_rich <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ angle_s * stimulus + trial_s +
    (1 + angle_s + trial_s | user_id) +
    (1 | item),
  data = mrot_rich_data,
  control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 20000))
)

# extract subject-level random effects
ran_effs <- ranef(m_rich)$user_id %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("user_id") %>%
  rename(
    int_dev   = `(Intercept)`,
    slope_dev = angle_s,
    trial_dev = trial_s
  )

# fixed effects (global averages)
fix_int <- fixef(m_rich)["(Intercept)"]
fix_ang <- fixef(m_rich)["angle_s"]
fix_tri <- fixef(m_rich)["trial_s"]

# compute cognitive features (on log-RT scale)
rich_features_raw <- ran_effs %>%
  mutate(
    # Baseline Speed: Speed at angle 0 (Intercept)
    Baseline_Speed = fix_int + int_dev,
    # Absolute Slope: Time added per degree of rotation (Rotation Cost)
    Abs_Slope = fix_ang + slope_dev,
    # Relative Slope (Per Mike's suggestion)
    # "Is rotation expensive relative to their normal speed?"
    Rel_Slope = Abs_Slope / Baseline_Speed,
    # Learning Rate 
    Learning_Rate  = fix_tri + trial_dev
  )
# compute instability (Residual SD)
# We calculate SD of the *residuals* (not raw RT) to remove the "Task Difficulty" confound.
# This isolates internal inconsistency from the fact that some kids saw harder items.
mrot_rich_data$resid <- residuals(m_rich)

instability_data <- mrot_rich_data %>%
  group_by(site, user_id) %>%
  summarise(
    # Instability = SD of residuals (pure internal noise)
    Instability = sd(resid, na.rm = TRUE), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

user_site_map <- mrot_rt_trial_no_retest %>%
  distinct(site, user_id)

# join
rich_features_final <- rich_features_raw %>%
  left_join(user_site_map, by = "user_id") %>%
  left_join(instability_data, by = c("site", "user_id")) %>% 
  left_join(ability_user,  by = c("site", "user_id")) %>%
  mutate(
    Site = str_replace_all(site, c("pilot_" = "", "_" = "-"))
  ) %>%
  # Filter to ensure all needed features
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Baseline_Speed, Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite))
```

```{r}
#| label: clustering-execution
#| include: false

my_colors <- c(
  "Ineffective Strategies" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[1], # red
  "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[2], # blue
  "Mental Rotation" = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set1")[3]  # green
)

analysis_data <- rich_features_final %>%
  filter(if_all(c(ability, Baseline_Speed, Abs_Slope, Rel_Slope, 
                  Instability, Learning_Rate), is.finite)) 

global_input <- analysis_data %>%
  select(Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, 
         Instability, Learning_Rate) %>%
  scale()

set.seed(123)
k_global <- kmeans(global_input, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
analysis_data$Global_Cluster <- as.factor(k_global$cluster)

cluster_stats <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Global_Cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ability = mean(ability),
    mean_slope   = mean(Rel_Slope), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# FIX: as.character() on all pull() calls
low_eff_id <- cluster_stats %>%
  arrange(mean_ability) %>% 
  slice(1) %>% 
  pull(Global_Cluster) %>%
  as.character()

effective_clusters <- cluster_stats %>%
  filter(as.character(Global_Cluster) != low_eff_id) %>%
  arrange(mean_slope) 

analytical_id <- effective_clusters %>%
  slice(1) %>% 
  pull(Global_Cluster) %>%
  as.character()

holistic_id <- effective_clusters %>%
  slice(2) %>% 
  pull(Global_Cluster) %>%
  as.character()

analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(Strategy_Label = case_when(
    as.character(Global_Cluster) == low_eff_id    ~ "Ineffective Strategies",
    as.character(Global_Cluster) == analytical_id ~ "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)",
    as.character(Global_Cluster) == holistic_id   ~ "Mental Rotation"
  ),
  Strategy_Label = factor(Strategy_Label, levels = names(my_colors)))

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = ability, y = Rel_Slope, color = Strategy_Label)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = my_colors) +
  labs(title = "Cluster Result: Ability vs. Relative Slope")
```

## Exploratory: Strategy Identification via Clustering

Our third research question asked, exploratorily, whether meaningful variation in how children engage with the spatial demands of the task can be identified from trial-level behavioral signatures. We approach this as an attempt to characterize a continuum of engagement rather than identify discrete strategy types — from children who appear to disengage from the spatial structure of the task entirely, to those who engage effectively in varying ways. We use k-means clustering (k = 3) to identify convenient regions of this continuum for interpretive purposes, while noting that the clusters are inferred from behavioral proxies rather than directly observed strategies. The solution is sensitive to analytic choices, and replication in larger samples is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn.

To characterize individual differences in how children approach the task, we fitted a mixed-effects model predicting log-RT from rotation angle, stimulus type, their interaction, and trial number, with by-participant random intercepts and slopes for angle and trial number, and a random intercept by item. From this model we extracted four person-level features for each child: baseline response speed, absolute RT–angle slope, RT–angle slope relative to baseline speed, and trial-by-trial RT trend (learning rate). We additionally computed response instability as the standard deviation of model residuals, capturing trial-to-trial variability in RT not explained by item properties. 

These features were submitted to k-means clustering (k = 3), chosen on both theoretical grounds, as k = 2 collapsed two qualitatively distinct effective engagement profiles into a single cluster (see @apx-cluster-summary-stats) and on empirical grounds — the elbow method showed a moderate inflection at k = 3 (see @apx-cluster). Cluster labels were assigned based on mean ability and relative slope as convenient anchors on the engagement continuum: a low-ability cluster with a near-zero RT–angle slope was labeled 'Ineffective Strategies' (n = `r ineff$N`); of the remaining two clusters, the one with the steeper RT–angle slope was labeled 'Mental Rotation' (n = `r mrot_strat$N`); and the cluster with the shallower slope and higher mean ability was labeled 'Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)' (n = `r flip$N`).

The three clusters showed clearly differentiated profiles on both defining dimensions (@fig-validation-boxplots). Ability differed across all pairwise comparisons (all *p*s < .0001), with the Ineffective Strategies group showing markedly lower ability (M = `r round(ineff$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(ineff$SD_Ability, 2)`) than both the Flipping/Matching (M = `r round(flip$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(flip$SD_Ability, 2)`) and Mental Rotation (M = `r round(mrot_strat$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(mrot_strat$SD_Ability, 2)`) groups. Relative RT slope also differed significantly across all pairwise comparisons (all *p*s < .001), with the Mental Rotation cluster showing the steepest slope (M = `r round(mrot_strat$Mean_Slope, 2)`), consistent with analog rotation processes that scale with angular disparity.

Inspection of the RT–angle functions (@fig-rt-by-disparity) reveals qualitatively distinct profiles across the three groups. The Ineffective Strategies group (n = `r ineff$N`) is characterized by very low ability (M = `r round(ineff$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(ineff$SD_Ability, 2)`), a flat or slightly negative RT–angle slope (M = `r round(ineff$Mean_Slope, 2)`), and high response instability (M = `r round(ineff$Mean_Instab, 2)`). This group's RT decreases with rotation angle — 
they respond more quickly to harder items, not more slowly. Combined with steeply declining accuracy (@fig-accuracy-by-angle), this pattern suggests these children are not engaging with the spatial structure of the items, and may be disengaging at higher angular disparities. This is a qualitatively different failure mode from simply being slow.

The Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching) group (n = `r flip$N`) is the largest cluster and shows the highest mean ability (M = `r round(flip$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(flip$SD_Ability, 2)`). Note that although this group's absolute RT values are higher than the Mental Rotation group throughout (as visible in @fig-rt-by-disparity), this reflects slower baseline processing speed rather than greater rotation cost — the Mental Rotation group's steeper relative slope indicates greater RT increase as a proportion of their baseline speed. Their RT–angle function rises to a peak around 120° before declining at 160°, consistent with exploiting reflective symmetry at high angular disparities rather than performing full analog rotation — a pattern sometimes described as "flipping" in the mental rotation literature — as items approach 180°, mirror images become easier to distinguish perceptually without requiring full rotation. Their sustained accuracy across angles supports this interpretation: this is a genuinely effective strategy, not a speed-accuracy trade-off. 

The Mental Rotation group (n = `r mrot_strat$N`) shows the classic monotonically increasing RT–angle function consistent with the Shepard-Metzler signature, with the steepest relative slope of the three groups (M = `r round(mrot_strat$Mean_Slope, 2)`, SD = `r round(mrot_strat$SD_Slope, 2)`). Interestingly, this group has lower mean ability 
than the Flipping/Matching group (M = `r round(mrot_strat$Mean_Ability, 2)`, SD = `r round(mrot_strat$SD_Ability, 2)`), despite appearing to use the strategy the task was designed to elicit. This may reflect the greater cognitive cost of analog rotation relative to feature-matching strategies, particularly for the 2D stimuli where rotational demands are lower.

Taken together, these profiles offer one possible explanation for the attenuated angular disparity effect observed for 2D stimuli reported earlier: the flatter RT–angle functions may partly reflect the predominance of feature-matching strategies in the sample, with only a minority of children showing clear evidence of analog rotation. This interpretation is speculative, however, as the clustering was not performed separately by stimulus type.

### Strategy Use Across Age Groups

As a final component of our exploratory third research question, we examined whether the distribution of strategy clusters varied across age groups (@fig-strategy-by-age). We emphasize that this analysis is purely descriptive — cell sizes are too small for formal inferential testing, and the cluster solution itself carries the caveats described above. With those caveats in mind, a descriptive pattern is nonetheless visible. The proportion of children assigned to the Ineffective Strategies cluster declined substantially with age, from `r get_prop("[5,7]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% in the youngest group (ages 5–7) to `r get_prop("(7,9]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% (ages 7–9) and `r get_prop("(9,12]", "Ineffective Strategies") * 100`% (ages 9–12). This was accompanied by a corresponding increase in the Flipping/Matching cluster, from `r get_prop("[5,7]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`% to `r get_prop("(7,9]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`% and `r get_prop("(9,12]", "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)") * 100`%. By contrast, the proportion assigned to the Mental Rotation cluster remained strikingly stable across age groups (`r get_prop("[5,7]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%, `r get_prop("(7,9]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%, `r get_prop("(9,12]", "Mental Rotation") * 100`%). The primary developmental shift between ages 5 and 12 thus appears to be a move away from task disengagement toward effective feature-matching strategies, rather than an increase in full analog rotation. Whether this reflects a genuine developmental trajectory or an artifact of the clustering solution warrants investigation in larger samples.

```{r}
vars <- c("Baseline_Speed", "Rel_Slope", "Abs_Slope", "Instability", "Learning_Rate")

stopifnot(all(vars %in% names(analysis_data)))
stopifnot(all(c("Site", "user_id", "Strategy_Label") %in% names(analysis_data)))
stopifnot(nrow(analysis_data) == nrow(dplyr::distinct(analysis_data, Site, user_id)))

# ARI function
ARI <- function(a, b) {
  a <- as.integer(factor(a))
  b <- as.integer(factor(b))
  tab <- table(a, b)
  n <- sum(tab)
  if (n <= 1) return(NA_real_)
  comb2    <- function(x) x * (x - 1) / 2
  sum_ij   <- sum(comb2(tab))
  sum_i    <- sum(comb2(rowSums(tab)))
  sum_j    <- sum(comb2(colSums(tab)))
  expected <- (sum_i * sum_j) / comb2(n)
  max_idx  <- 0.5 * (sum_i + sum_j)
  denom    <- max_idx - expected
  if (denom == 0) return(NA_real_)
  (sum_ij - expected) / denom
}

get_local_strategy_labels <- function(df_site,
                                      k = 3,
                                      seed = 123,
                                      nstart = 25,
                                      min_n = 30) {

  if (nrow(df_site) < min_n) return(NULL)
  set.seed(seed)

  X <- df_site %>%
    dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(vars)) %>%
    scale() %>%
    as.matrix()

  km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = nstart)

  tmp <- df_site %>%
    mutate(Local_Cluster = factor(km$cluster))

  local_stats <- tmp %>%
    group_by(Local_Cluster) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_abil  = mean(ability,   na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_slope = mean(Rel_Slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(mean_abil)

  ineff_id     <- local_stats %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()
  other_two    <- local_stats %>% filter(as.character(Local_Cluster) != ineff_id) %>% arrange(mean_slope)
  other_eff_id <- other_two   %>% slice(1) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()
  mrot_id      <- other_two   %>% slice(2) %>% pull(Local_Cluster) %>% as.character()

  tmp %>%
    mutate(
      Strategy_Local = dplyr::case_when(
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == ineff_id     ~ "Ineffective Strategies",
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == other_eff_id ~ "Other Effective Strategies (Flipping/Matching)",
        as.character(Local_Cluster) == mrot_id      ~ "Mental Rotation"
      ),
      Strategy_Local = factor(Strategy_Local, levels = levels(analysis_data$Strategy_Label))
    ) %>%
    select(Site, user_id, Strategy_Local)
}

# fit local models independently within each site
local_labels_all <- analysis_data %>%
  group_by(Site) %>%
  group_split() %>%
  purrr::map_dfr(get_local_strategy_labels)

analysis_local <- analysis_data %>%
  select(-dplyr::any_of("Strategy_Local")) %>%
  left_join(local_labels_all, by = c("Site", "user_id"))

# agreement (3-class)
agreement_3class <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  group_by(Site) %>%
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    pct_agree = mean(Strategy_Local == Strategy_Label),
    ARI       = ARI(Strategy_Label, Strategy_Local),
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

agreement_3class

# confusion matrices per site — save split first to avoid pipe . scoping issue
site_splits <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  group_split(Site)

confusion_by_site <- site_splits %>%
  purrr::set_names(purrr::map_chr(site_splits, ~ unique(.x$Site))) %>%
  purrr::map(~ table(.x$Strategy_Local, .x$Strategy_Label))

confusion_by_site

# recall + purity
recall_tbl <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  count(Site, Strategy_Label, Strategy_Local) %>%
  group_by(Site, Strategy_Label) %>%
  mutate(recall = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

purity_tbl <- analysis_local %>%
  filter(!is.na(Strategy_Local)) %>%
  count(Site, Strategy_Local, Strategy_Label) %>%
  group_by(Site, Strategy_Local) %>%
  mutate(purity = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

diag_summary <- recall_tbl %>%
  filter(Strategy_Label == Strategy_Local) %>%
  transmute(Site, Strategy = Strategy_Label, recall) %>%
  left_join(
    purity_tbl %>%
      filter(Strategy_Local == Strategy_Label) %>%
      transmute(Site, Strategy = Strategy_Local, purity),
    by = c("Site", "Strategy")
  )

diag_summary
```

```{r}
get_diag <- function(site, label) {
  out <- diag_summary[diag_summary$Site == site & diag_summary$Strategy == label, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(out) == 0) {
    return(data.frame(Site = site, Strategy = label, recall = NA_real_, purity = NA_real_))
  }
  stopifnot(nrow(out) == 1)
  out
}

# off-diagonal moves
get_move <- function(tab, local_lab, global_lab) {
  stopifnot(local_lab %in% rownames(tab), global_lab %in% colnames(tab))
  n     <- tab[local_lab, global_lab]
  denom <- sum(tab[, global_lab])
  list(n = as.numeric(n), denom = as.numeric(denom), prop = as.numeric(n) / as.numeric(denom))
}
```

### Robustness checks
To assess the robustness of the identified continuum structure, we conducted three additional checks reported in full in the appendices. First, silhouette analysis favored k=2 while the elbow method showed a moderate inflection at k=3; examination of the k=2 solution confirmed that it collapsed two qualitatively distinct RT–angle profiles, justifying the adoption of k=3 (see @apx-cluster). Second, dimensionality reduction using PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP consistently recovered the separation of the Ineffective Strategies group from the two effective engagement profiles, while the boundary between the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching groups was substantially less clear across all three methods — providing direct visual support for the continuum interpretation (see @apx-dimreduc). Third, re-plotting RT and accuracy functions using the full 0–360° rotation angles provided direct support for the assumption that participants rotate stimuli via the shortest available path: both effective engagement profiles showed near-symmetric inverted-U RT functions peaking around 200–240° before declining as angles approached 360°, consistent with shortest-path rotation throughout. The flipping signature of the Flipping/Matching group was again evident, and the Ineffective Strategies group continued to show a broadly decreasing RT function with accuracy near chance at peak angles, replicating the main analysis findings under this alternative parameterization (see @apx-360-angle).

### Cross-Cultural Consistency of Strategy Clusters
We next examined whether the continuum structure is recoverable within each site independently by re-running the k-means procedure separately within each site and computing agreement between the local and global solutions using percent agreement and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). The most fundamental distinction — between children who disengage from the spatial structure of the task and those who engage effectively — was recovered consistently across all three sites. The Ineffective Strategies and Flipping/Matching clusters showed moderate-to-good local recovery across sites (Canada: `r fmt_pct(a_wes$pct_agree)`, ARI = `r fmt_num(a_wes$ARI)`; Colombia: `r fmt_pct(a_uni$pct_agree)`, ARI = `r fmt_num(a_uni$ARI)`; Germany: `r fmt_pct(a_mpi$pct_agree)`, ARI = `r fmt_num(a_mpi$ARI)`); Germany's lower percent agreement despite its larger sample may reflect greater RT variability introduced by its remote home-based testing format.

The finer-grained boundary between the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching clusters was less stable: the Mental Rotation cluster was not independently recoverable in Germany or Canada, where locally-clustered children predominantly mapped onto the Flipping/Matching group instead. Colombia showed the most consistent local recovery across all three regions of the continuum. These findings reinforce the interpretation that what is robustly recoverable across cultural contexts is the broad distinction between disengagement and effective spatial engagement — not the finer subdivision within the effective end of the continuum.

# Discussion

The central aim of this study was to establish whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task measures the same underlying construct across three culturally diverse sites. The answer, across three distinct levels of analysis, is largely yes. The task achieves scalar measurement invariance indicating that its psychometric structure is consistent across cultural contexts. The canonical angular disparity effect replicates across all three sites for 3D stimuli, providing process-level evidence that performance is driven by the spatial demands of the task in the way theory predicts [@shepard1971mental]. And at the level of individual behavioral profiles, the broad distinction between children who engage with the spatial structure of the task and those who do not is recoverable within each site independently. That these three forms of convergent evidence emerge across geographically and culturally diverse samples extends the cross-cultural generalizability of mental rotation research beyond the predominantly Western samples in which most developmental work has been conducted [@davis2021cultural; @henrich2010weirdest], and supports the interpretation that the task is capturing a genuinely spatial construct rather than one that is specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was developed.

## Measurement Invariance
Turning to our first research question, the demonstration of scalar invariance under a 2PL model establishes that the mental rotation task functions comparably across pilot sites — that items are ordered by difficulty in the same way for children in Bogotá as for children in Leipzig or Ontario, and that ability estimates can be placed on a common latent scale [@putnick2016measurement]. This finding is meaningful in that tasks developed in Western contexts and subsequently exported to non-Western settings do not automatically achieve psychometric equivalence; apparent performance differences can reflect differences in task familiarity or culturally-specific knowledge rather than the target construct itself [@van2004bias]. The fact that scalar invariance holds here suggests the LEVANTE mental rotation task is not heavily dependent on such factors — the same item features drive difficulty in a similar way regardless of cultural context. This provides a necessary foundation for the analyses that follow, but it also carries a broader implication: with appropriate localization and piloting, spatial cognitive tasks developed in Western samples can achieve genuine psychometric equivalence across diverse populations of children. It should be noted that scalar invariance establishes metric comparability rather than cultural equivalence in any deeper sense. It does not indicate that mental rotation ability is equally developed across sites, and given that LEVANTE sites differ substantially in sampling, recruitment, and testing format, site-level performance differences are not interpreted here.

## Angular Disparity and Process-Level Validity
Our second research question asked whether performance is driven by the spatial properties of the stimuli in the way theory predicts. The key benchmark here is the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental: as the rotational distance between a 3D target and its match increases, so too does the time required to judge whether they correspond. This relationship — among the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology [@cooper1973chronometric; @peters2008applications] — has been demonstrated extensively in Western adult samples, but its replication across culturally diverse samples of children had not previously been established. Its consistent emergence here, across all three sites, suggests that the underlying cognitive process it indexes — the spatially continuous transformation of object orientation — is not specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was originally documented. This matters because psychometric equivalence and process-level validity are distinct forms of evidence. It is one thing to show that a task achieves comparable difficulty ordering across sites; it is another to show that performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of the stimuli in precisely the way that mental rotation theory predicts. The angular disparity effect provides the latter, and its cross-cultural replication substantially strengthens the case that the task is engaging spatial cognition specifically, rather than some culturally-variable combination of task-general skills.

The picture for 2D stimuli requires more nuance. Formal modelling confirmed a significant positive angle effect for both 3D (β = `r round(beta_3d_comb, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_3d_comb, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_3d_main)`) and 2D stimuli (β = `r round(beta_2d_comb, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_2d_main, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(p_2d_main)`), and a combined model confirmed that the angle slope was significantly steeper for 3D than 2D items (β difference = `r round(beta_diff, 2)`, SE = `r round(se_diff, 2)`, χ²(`r anova_combined_df`) = `r round(anova_combined_chisq, 2)`, p `r fmt_p(anova_combined_p)`). This attenuation suggests that the underlying rotation process is engaged by 2D stimuli, but less consistently or completely than for 3D geometric shapes. Two complementary accounts from the adult literature help explain why. @folk1987effects showed that when stimuli are easy to discriminate, solvers can make same/different judgments by comparing surface features without rotating at all, producing shallower RT–angle functions. @bethell1988mental showed that even when rotation does occur, familiar stimuli are transformed as integrated wholes rather than piece by piece, producing faster and less angle-sensitive responses than unfamiliar stimuli. Duck and rabbit silhouettes are both highly familiar to young children and relatively easy to discriminate, making them susceptible to both effects simultaneously. The 3D geometric shapes, by contrast, are genuinely unfamiliar and harder to discriminate, which likely drives children toward the full spatially continuous rotation process that produces the stronger RT–angle signature. Importantly, the significant 2D effect should be interpreted with caution: the 2D trial count (n = `r nrow(mrot_2d)`) is approximately three times larger than the 3D count (n = `r nrow(mrot_3d)`), giving substantially greater power to detect small effects. That said, the presence of even an attenuated angle effect across all three sites for 2D stimuli strengthens rather than undermines the overall cross-cultural generalizability argument: spatial sensitivity in children's mental rotation performance is detectable across cultural contexts even with simpler stimuli, though its magnitude depends on the rotational demands imposed by the task.

## Within-Task Dynamics
A complementary finding from the within-task dynamics analysis further extends the picture of cross-cultural consistency established by the first two research questions, asking whether children are sensitive to task demands as they unfold in real time rather than simply to the spatial properties of individual stimuli. Two patterns emerged consistently across all three sites. First, there was a pronounced jump in residual reaction times at the transition from 2D to 3D stimuli, and this increase was immediate rather than gradual — suggesting that children recalibrate their processing demands at the block boundary rather than adapting incrementally. This is consistent with the between-stimulus difference established in the angular disparity analysis and extends it: children appear sensitive to the qualitative shift in task demands imposed by 3D stimuli, and this sensitivity is cross-culturally robust. Second, within each block, reaction times decreased across trials, indicating a practice effect that operates independently of angular disparity. This is notable given the flat RT-angle functions observed for 2D stimuli: children are getting faster with practice on these items even in the absence of a detectable rotation effect, suggesting that practice-related acceleration and angular disparity sensitivity are capturing distinct aspects of performance. The cross-cultural consistency of both patterns — the block transition jump and the within-block acceleration — extends the picture of convergence established by the measurement invariance and angular disparity analyses, suggesting that not only the psychometric structure and the core cognitive signature of mental rotation, but also the real-time dynamics of task engagement, are broadly stable across cultural contexts.

## Cognitive Strategy Profiles
Our third research question asked whether meaningful variation in how children engage with the spatial demands of the task can be identified from trial-level behavioral signatures. Research with adults has established that solvers draw on a range of strategies when performing mental rotation tasks, spanning a holistic-analytic continuum [@gluck2003spatial], and that strategy selection varies across individuals and shifts with task demands [@nazareth2019strategy]. Crucially, such strategies can be identified from behavioral signatures in RT data even in the absence of direct observation [@geiser2006separating], providing the methodological basis for the present analysis. The clustering analysis suggests that children's behavioral profiles are better understood as distributed along a continuum than as falling into discrete strategy types. At one end of this continuum, a subset of children — labeled Ineffective Strategies — show clear disengagement from the spatial structure of the task: flat or declining RT–angle slopes, high response instability, and near-chance accuracy at high angular disparities. At the other end, children engage effectively with the task, though they vary in the form that engagement takes. 

The clustering analysis suggests that children's behavioral profiles are better understood as distributed along a continuum than as falling into discrete strategy types. At one end of this continuum, a subset of children — labeled Ineffective Strategies — show clear disengagement from the spatial structure of the task: flat or declining RT–angle slopes, high response instability, and near-chance accuracy at high angular disparities. At the other end, children engage effectively with the task, though they vary in the form that engagement takes.

The Flipping/Matching group — the largest cluster — shows an inverted-U RT–angle function consistent with exploiting reflective symmetry at high angular disparities, a genuinely effective approach reflected in their sustained accuracy across angles. The Mental Rotation group shows the classic monotonically increasing RT–angle function consistent with spatially continuous rotation, but has lower mean ability than the Flipping/Matching group — likely reflecting the greater cognitive cost of full analog rotation relative to feature-matching strategies [@just1985cognitive; @khooshabeh2013individual], particularly for the 2D stimuli where rotational demands are lower. Importantly, these two effective profiles occupy overlapping regions of the behavioral feature space across all three dimensionality reduction methods.

The finding that the Mental Rotation cluster was not independently recoverable in Germany or Canada raises a question that goes beyond simple instability. One interpretation is that the Mental Rotation cluster as identified in the global solution is not a robust feature of the data — that it emerges from the particular composition of the pooled sample rather than reflecting a genuine and replicable behavioral profile. The continuum framing we adopt is partly motivated by this concern: rather than claiming the Mental Rotation cluster represents a discrete and recoverable strategy type, we treat it as a convenient marker of one end of the effective-engagement spectrum. The robustness evidence does, however, support retaining the distinction in the global solution, since collapsing to k=2 obscures a theoretically meaningful difference in RT–angle profile shape even if that difference does not crystallize into a separable cluster within individual sites. Colombia showed the most consistent local recovery across all three regions of the continuum, though given its distinctive sampling profile this should not be over-interpreted. Future work with larger site-specific samples is needed to determine whether the failure to recover the Mental Rotation cluster within Germany and Canada reflects a genuine difference in the distribution of engagement profiles across sites, or simply insufficient power to detect a minority profile at the sample sizes available here.

## Limitations
Several limitations of the present study warrant acknowledgment. First, our analyses is limited to a single task from the LEVANTE battery, and it remains to be seen whether the patterns of cross-cultural consistency observed here extend to other spatial tasks, or whether they are specific to mental rotation. Second, the sample spans ages 5–12 but the youngest age group showed more irregular patterns, particularly for 3D stimuli, likely reflecting limited sample sizes at the lower age range rather than a substantively different developmental trajectory. Future work with larger samples of younger children would help clarify the developmental onset of the cross-cultural signatures observed here. Finally, the strategy clustering analysis is exploratory and should be treated with caution. The clusters are inferred from behavioral proxies rather than directly observed strategies. More fundamentally, the failure to recover the Mental Rotation cluster independently in Germany or Canada raises the possibility that it is not a robust feature of the data, but an artifact of the pooled sample composition. This means that conclusions about strategy distributions and their cultural variation should be treated as tentative until replicated in larger, site-specific samples. 

# Conclusion

Three research questions motivated this study, each asking in a different way whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task is doing consistent and interpretable work across culturally diverse settings. Across all three, the answer is largely affirmative. These findings do not mean that mental rotation development is uniform across children or contexts — the substantial individual variability within sites, and the tentative evidence for cross-cultural differences in strategy distributions, suggest there is much still to understand about what drives variation in spatial ability across children. But they do mean that the task is measuring something real and consistent — that when a child in Bogotá and a child in Leipzig and a child in Ontario sit down to judge whether two objects match, they are, by and large, engaging the same cognitive process. That is a necessary foundation for the kind of cross-cultural developmental science that the LEVANTE project aims to build.

```{r}
  tab_spanner(label = "Relative Slope",  columns = c(`Mean Rel. Slope`, `SD Rel. Slope`)) %>%
  tab_spanner(label = "Absolute Slope",  columns = c(`Mean Abs. Slope`, `SD Abs. Slope`)) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.width = pct(100),
    data_row.padding = px(3)
  )
```

# Cluster Solution Validation {.appendix #apx-cluster}
To assess the appropriateness of the three-cluster solution, we evaluated cluster quality across k = 1–8 using two complementary metrics: total within-cluster sum of squares (the elbow method) and average silhouette width (@fig-k-sweep-validation). The silhouette analysis identified k = 2 as the statistically optimal solution, with average silhouette width peaking at 0.35 before declining steeply at k = 3 and remaining low thereafter. The elbow plot showed a moderate inflection at k = 3, after which additional clusters yielded diminishing reductions in within-cluster variance. To interrogate whether k = 2 was substantively adequate, we examined the RT–angle functions of the resulting two-cluster solution (@fig-k2-cluster-check). The higher-ability cluster displayed a characteristic inverted-U RT function, rising to a peak around 120° before declining at 160° — a pattern that, in the three-cluster solution, distinguishes the Flipping/Matching and Mental Rotation groups. This indicates that k = 2 collapses two qualitatively distinct effective strategies into a single cluster, obscuring a theoretically meaningful behavioral difference. We therefore adopted k = 3 on both empirical grounds (the elbow inflection) and theoretical grounds (the interpretability of the resulting RT profiles).

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "**Cluster validation metrics: Elbow Method (left) and Silhouette Analysis (right).** The elbow plot shows a bend at k=3, and silhouette width peaks at k=2 before declining, providing partial support for the 3-cluster solution."

p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "wss", k.max = 8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = 2, color = pal$red) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k")

p_sil <- fviz_nbclust(global_input, kmeans, method = "silhouette", k.max = 8) +
  labs(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL, x = "Number of clusters k")

grid.arrange(p_elbow, p_sil, nrow = 1)
```

```{r}
# --- 2. Run K-Means with K=2 ---

# The other one is High Efficiency
```

# Dimensionality Reduction Checks {.appendix #apx-dimreduc}
To further validate the cluster structure, we examined whether the three-cluster solution was recoverable using alternative dimensionality reduction methods: PCA (@fig-pca-check), t-SNE (@fig-tsne-check), and UMAP (@fig-umap-check). PCA loadings were also inspected to characterize the underlying feature structure (@fig-pca-loadings).

Results were consistent across all three methods in one key respect: the Ineffective Strategies group was clearly and reliably separated from the two effective strategy groups, appearing as a distinct region in all three projections — the top-left in the t-SNE, the negative end of PC1 in the PCA, and the bottom-left in the UMAP. This convergent separation provides strong evidence that this group occupies a genuinely distinct region of the feature space. The boundary between the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching groups was, however, substantially less clear. Green and blue points overlapped considerably across all three visualizations, suggesting these two groups may represent ends of a continuum rather than fully discrete clusters — a finding consistent with the silhouette analysis favouring k = 2.

Inspection of the PCA loadings offered interpretive support for the feature set. PC1 loaded positively on Baseline Speed, Learning Rate, and Absolute Slope, and negatively on Instability, reflecting a general processing efficiency dimension: children who respond faster, improve more across trials, and show less trial-to-trial noise score higher on this component. PC2 loaded most strongly on Relative Slope and Absolute Slope — both positive — and negatively on Learning Rate, reflecting a rotation cost dimension that is largely independent of general speed. The fact that these two components map onto theoretically meaningful and distinct dimensions provides confidence that the clustering features are not redundant.
```{r}
#| label: fig-tsne-check
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "**t-SNE visualization of strategy clusters.** The Ineffective Strategies group forms a distinct region in the top-left, while the Mental Rotation and Flipping/Matching groups show considerable overlap in the central and right regions, suggesting softer boundaries between the two effective strategy groups."

library(Rtsne)

    select(user_id, Learning_Rate, Baseline_Speed, Rel_Slope, Abs_Slope, Instability) %>%

    as.matrix(tsne_input %>% select(-user_id)), 
    dims = 2, 
    perplexity = 30, 
    verbose = FALSE, 
    max_iter = 500
)

tsne_plot_data <- tsne_input %>%
    mutate(
        tSNE_1 = tsne_result$Y[,1],
        tSNE_2 = tsne_result$Y[,2]
    ) %>%
    left_join(analysis_data %>% select(user_id, Strategy_Label), by = "user_id")

ggplot(tsne_plot_data, aes(x = tSNE_1, y = tSNE_2, color = Strategy_Label)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +

    labs(
        title = NULL,
        x = "Dimension 1",
        y = "Dimension 2",
        color = "Strategy"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
